title: Hypertension: Measure, Trend, and Protect Organs
clientNeeds: Health Promotion and Maintenance
Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological Therapies
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Hypertension management starts with accurate repeat measurement and trends, not one rushed reading. Severe blood pressure without acute target-organ injury is different from hypertensive emergency; new neurologic, cardiac, renal, retinal, or aortic injury changes the priority to urgent escalation.
recognize: Hypertension is often asymptomatic, so symptoms should not be required before taking a high reading seriously.
The 2025 U.S. guideline retains normal <120/80, elevated 120-129/<80, stage 1 at 130-139 or 80-89, and stage 2 at 140 or higher or 90 or higher.
Headache alone does not prove hypertensive emergency; look for acute organ injury.
priorities: Repeat abnormal blood pressure using correct cuff size and positioning.
Assess medication adherence, orthostatic symptoms, pain/anxiety, stimulant/decongestant use, and signs of acute target-organ injury.
Escalate immediately for severe hypertension with focal neurologic deficit, ischemic chest pain, pulmonary edema, aortic symptoms, acute kidney injury, or encephalopathy.
assessMonitor: Trend home and clinical blood pressure when ordered, orthostatic symptoms, renal function, potassium, edema, and medication adverse effects.
For treated adults, a common guideline target is below 130/80 mm Hg when appropriate and tolerated, with individualization for frailty, institutional care, pregnancy, or limited life expectancy.
interventions: Reinforce DASH-style eating patterns, lower sodium intake, physical activity, weight management when relevant, alcohol reduction, smoking cessation, and medication adherence.
Support home blood pressure monitoring with a validated upper-arm device and correct technique.
medicationSafety: ACE inhibitors and ARBs can cause hyperkalemia and renal function changes and are contraindicated in pregnancy.
Diuretics may cause electrolyte depletion or volume depletion.
Beta blockers and some calcium-channel blockers can cause bradycardia or hypotension depending on agent.
redFlags: Markedly reduced urine output with severe hypertension
teaching: Teach that consistent treatment prevents silent organ damage even when the patient feels well.
Bring home readings and medication list to follow-up visits.
delegationScope: Routine blood pressure measurement may be delegated when the patient is stable and reporting thresholds are explicit.
The PN evaluates unexpected readings and symptoms within scope and escalates acute target-organ findings.
examTrap: Treating an isolated high number aggressively before repeating the measurement and assessing for organ injury.
oneLinePearl: Measure correctly, trend the pressure, and look for organ injury before deciding urgency.
sourceBasis: 2025 AHA/ACC Multisociety High Blood Pressure Guideline

title: Peripheral Artery Disease: Perfusion Before Compression
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Health Promotion and Maintenance
bottomLine: Peripheral artery disease reduces limb perfusion. Exertional calf pain relieved by rest suggests claudication; sudden pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, or poikilothermia suggests acute limb ischemia and requires immediate escalation.
recognize: Chronic findings include diminished pulses, cool skin, dependent rubor, shiny hairless skin, delayed healing, and distal ulcers.
Rest pain, especially at night or with elevation, suggests more severe ischemia.
Smoking, diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and older age increase risk.
priorities: Assess color, temperature, capillary refill, pulses, pain pattern, sensation, motor function, and wounds.
Escalate acute loss of perfusion immediately.
Protect ischemic feet from trauma and pressure.
assessMonitor: Trend walking tolerance, wound healing, pulses, skin integrity, and cardiovascular risk-factor control.
Ankle-brachial index and vascular imaging may be ordered to define disease severity.
interventions: Encourage structured walking exercise when stable and prescribed.
Support smoking cessation and foot protection.
Positioning should preserve perfusion; avoid unnecessary elevation of a severely ischemic limb.
medicationSafety: Antiplatelet and lipid-lowering therapies are commonly used for cardiovascular risk reduction; monitor for bleeding or medication adverse effects.
Compression therapy should not be applied reflexively to an ischemic limb without confirming arterial status and orders.
teaching: Inspect feet daily, wear protective footwear, avoid smoking, and report new wounds or rest pain early.
delegationScope: Routine foot hygiene can be delegated for stable patients with clear precautions.
New ischemic pain, color change, absent pulse, or wound deterioration requires licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Applying tight compression stockings to a cold pulseless leg because the patient also has edema.
oneLinePearl: PAD is a perfusion problem: cold, painful, pulseless changes outrank edema.
sourceBasis: 2024 ACC/AHA Lower Extremity Peripheral Artery Disease Guideline

title: Pericarditis and Tamponade: Pain vs Pressure
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Acute pericarditis often causes sharp pleuritic chest pain that improves sitting forward, but a growing pericardial effusion can progress to tamponade. Hypotension, tachycardia, rising JVP, muffled heart sounds, dyspnea, or pulsus paradoxus signal impaired cardiac filling and urgent deterioration.
recognize: Pericarditis pain may worsen with inspiration or lying flat and improve when sitting forward.
A pericardial friction rub can occur but its absence does not exclude disease.
Tamponade may present with anxiety, tachycardia, hypotension, jugular venous distention, dyspnea, and reduced heart sounds.
priorities: Assess ABCs, blood pressure, heart rate, oxygenation, neck veins, chest pain, and perfusion.
Escalate suspected tamponade immediately and prepare for urgent echocardiography/intervention.
Avoid unnecessary delays for routine diagnostics in an unstable patient.
assessMonitor: Trend hemodynamics, rhythm, respiratory status, pain, and signs of worsening effusion.
Monitor renal and GI risks when anti-inflammatory therapy is prescribed.
interventions: Position for comfort and reduced dyspnea.
Administer prescribed anti-inflammatory therapy for uncomplicated pericarditis and monitor response.
Support urgent pericardiocentesis or surgical management when tamponade is present.
medicationSafety: NSAIDs can worsen kidney injury, GI bleeding, and fluid retention in susceptible patients.
Anticoagulation decisions require clinician review when a significant pericardial effusion or bleeding risk exists.
redFlags: Narrowing pulse pressure with poor perfusion
teaching: Report increasing dyspnea, fainting, or new swelling rather than assuming recurrent pain is harmless.
delegationScope: New chest pain or hemodynamic change requires licensed-nurse assessment; do not delegate the evaluation of suspected tamponade.
examTrap: Treating worsening dyspnea and hypotension as anxiety because the patient already has a diagnosis of pericarditis.
oneLinePearl: Pericarditis hurts; tamponade compresses—falling pressure means escalate.
sourceBasis: 2025 ACC Expert Consensus Guidance on Pericarditis

title: Aortic Dissection: Sudden Pain, Pulse Difference, Emergency
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
bottomLine: Acute aortic dissection is a time-critical vascular emergency. Sudden severe chest, back, or abdominal pain with pulse/BP asymmetry, neurologic deficit, syncope, new aortic regurgitation murmur, or shock requires immediate emergency escalation and rapid definitive imaging/management.
recognize: Pain is often abrupt and maximal near onset rather than gradually building.
Hypertension, known aneurysm, connective-tissue disease, bicuspid aortic valve, stimulant use, and pregnancy-related aortic disease can increase risk.
A normal pulse exam does not exclude dissection.
priorities: Activate emergency response, keep the patient at rest, obtain bilateral arm pressures when feasible without delaying care, and assess pulses, neurologic status, perfusion, and pain.
Prepare for urgent imaging and IV anti-impulse therapy under acute-care orders.
Do not give anticoagulants or thrombolytics reflexively until competing aortic pathology is considered.
assessMonitor: Continuous blood pressure, rhythm, neurologic, urine-output, and perfusion monitoring in acute care.
interventions: Minimize exertion and sympathetic stimulation.
Support rapid transfer to a center capable of surgical/endovascular management when indicated.
medicationSafety: IV beta blockade is commonly used first for anti-impulse therapy when not contraindicated, followed by additional blood-pressure control as needed under specialist direction.
Anticoagulation or fibrinolysis can be catastrophic if dissection is mistaken for acute coronary syndrome.
redFlags: Sudden tearing or severe chest/back pain
teaching: Patients with known aortic disease should understand surveillance and emergency symptoms and avoid stopping antihypertensive therapy without guidance.
delegationScope: Suspected dissection is unstable; the PN initiates emergency measures within policy and escalates immediately.
examTrap: Giving thrombolytic therapy for chest pain before recognizing the pulse difference and abrupt tearing back pain.
oneLinePearl: Sudden maximal pain plus pulse or neuro difference: think aorta before anticoagulating.
sourceBasis: 2022 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Aortic Disease

title: Infective Endocarditis: Fever, Murmur, Embolic Clues
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Infective endocarditis can destroy valves and send septic emboli to the brain, kidneys, spleen, lungs, or extremities. Persistent fever in a patient with prosthetic valve/device, prior endocarditis, injection drug use, or recent bacteremia plus a new murmur or embolic findings deserves urgent evaluation and blood cultures before antibiotics when the patient is stable enough to obtain them without harmful delay.
recognize: Fever, fatigue, new or changing murmur, petechiae, splinter hemorrhages, embolic stroke, hematuria, or unexplained heart failure may occur.
Prosthetic valves, prior endocarditis, selected congenital heart disease, intracardiac devices, and injection drug use increase risk.
Right-sided disease can present with pulmonary septic emboli.
priorities: Assess hemodynamic status, neurologic findings, new heart-failure signs, fever pattern, and embolic symptoms.
Obtain ordered blood cultures before antibiotics when feasible in a stable patient.
Escalate acute heart failure, stroke symptoms, sepsis, or conduction changes promptly.
assessMonitor: Trend temperature, cultures, renal function, rhythm, neurologic status, heart-failure signs, and IV access complications during prolonged therapy.
interventions: Administer targeted IV antimicrobial therapy as ordered and preserve reliable vascular access.
Use meticulous line care and oral hygiene.
medicationSafety: Prolonged antimicrobial regimens require monitoring for renal, hepatic, hematologic, and infusion-related toxicity depending on agent.
Antibiotic prophylaxis is reserved for selected highest-risk cardiac conditions and procedures; it is not routine for every patient with a murmur.
teaching: Complete the full antimicrobial course, protect IV access, maintain oral health, and report new neurologic or heart-failure symptoms.
delegationScope: Routine temperature checks may be delegated with clear thresholds; new murmur, neuro change, or heart-failure signs require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Assuming every patient with valve disease needs antibiotics before every invasive procedure.
oneLinePearl: Endocarditis is valve infection plus embolic risk—watch the brain, heart, kidneys, and cultures.
sourceBasis: American Heart Association Infective Endocarditis Prevention and Scientific Advisory Resources

title: Chronic Kidney Disease: Protect Function and Watch Complications
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Health Promotion and Maintenance
Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological Therapies
bottomLine: CKD is chronic loss of kidney function and/or persistent kidney damage, but nursing priorities are the complications: fluid overload, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, anemia, mineral-bone disease, medication accumulation, and progression. Trends in eGFR, albuminuria, weight, blood pressure, potassium, and symptoms matter more than one isolated creatinine.
recognize: Early CKD may be asymptomatic.
Later findings can include fatigue, edema, pruritus, nausea, sleep disturbance, anemia, hypertension, and reduced appetite.
Diabetes and hypertension are major causes and cardiovascular risk is high.
priorities: Track blood pressure, volume status, daily weight when ordered, urine output changes, potassium, renal function, and medication safety.
Report progressive dyspnea, hyperkalemia symptoms, uremic confusion, or rapidly declining kidney function.
Avoid preventable nephrotoxins and dehydration unless a clinician-directed plan requires otherwise.
assessMonitor: Monitor eGFR, urine albumin, potassium, bicarbonate, hemoglobin, calcium/phosphate/PTH when ordered, and response to kidney-protective therapy.
Review all OTC drugs and supplements for renal risk.
interventions: Support individualized sodium, fluid, protein, potassium, and phosphorus plans rather than imposing a universal restrictive diet.
Promote blood pressure and diabetes control and smoking cessation.
medicationSafety: Many drugs require renal dose adjustment.
NSAIDs can worsen kidney function in susceptible patients.
ACE inhibitors/ARBs and other kidney-protective agents require potassium and renal monitoring rather than automatic discontinuation for small expected changes.
redFlags: Rapid unexplained fall in kidney function
teaching: Avoid unapproved NSAIDs, keep follow-up labs, know the kidney-safe medication plan, and report sudden weight gain, dyspnea, or major urine changes.
delegationScope: Weights and intake/output may be delegated with exact reporting thresholds; interpretation of kidney-function trends and new symptoms requires licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Telling every CKD patient to drink large amounts of fluid despite edema or heart failure.
oneLinePearl: CKD care is trend care: pressure, potassium, volume, anemia, and medications.
sourceBasis: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for Evaluation and Management of CKD

title: UTI and Pyelonephritis: Bladder Symptoms vs Systemic Infection
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Dysuria, frequency, and urgency without systemic illness fit lower UTI; fever, chills, flank pain, vomiting, hypotension, or toxicity suggest infection beyond the bladder and increase sepsis risk. Culture-directed therapy and source control matter more as illness becomes complicated.
recognize: Lower UTI commonly causes dysuria, frequency, urgency, and suprapubic discomfort.
Pyelonephritis often adds fever, flank pain/CVA tenderness, nausea, or systemic symptoms.
Older adults with delirium should be assessed for many causes; bacteriuria alone does not prove symptomatic UTI.
priorities: Assess vital signs, hydration, flank pain, urinary symptoms, pregnancy status, catheter/device history, obstruction risk, and sepsis signs.
Collect ordered urine testing before antibiotics when feasible without delaying care in an unstable patient.
Escalate hypotension, severe vomiting, obstruction, pregnancy with systemic illness, or sepsis.
assessMonitor: Trend temperature, pain, intake/output, renal function, culture results, and response to antibiotics.
Review prior resistant organisms and recent antibiotic exposure when available.
interventions: Administer prescribed antibiotics and fluids based on severity and patient factors.
Remove or replace unnecessary urinary catheters according to orders/policy and support source control when obstruction is present.
medicationSafety: Definitive therapy should narrow to culture susceptibilities when possible.
Renal function, allergies, drug interactions, pregnancy, and prior resistance influence antibiotic selection.
Clinically improving complicated UTI may be eligible for IV-to-oral transition when an effective oral agent is available.
teaching: Complete antibiotics as prescribed, hydrate according to the plan, and seek care for fever, flank pain, vomiting, or worsening symptoms.
delegationScope: Routine urine measurement may be delegated; new fever, flank pain, hypotension, or delirium requires licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Treating asymptomatic bacteriuria in every older adult as the cause of confusion without assessing other etiologies.
oneLinePearl: Bladder symptoms stay local; fever and flank pain mean think upper tract and sepsis.
sourceBasis: IDSA 2025 Guideline Update on Complicated Urinary Tract Infections

title: Kidney Stones: Pain, Obstruction, and Infection Risk
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Renal colic causes severe flank pain that may radiate to the groin, often with hematuria and nausea. The dangerous combination is obstruction plus infection: fever, chills, hypotension, rising creatinine, or anuria with a suspected stone requires urgent urologic escalation rather than routine outpatient pain management.
recognize: Patients with ureteral stones are often restless and unable to get comfortable, unlike classic peritoneal irritation where movement worsens pain.
Microscopic or visible hematuria may occur but can be absent.
Stone size, location, infection, renal function, and ability to control pain/vomiting determine disposition.
priorities: Assess pain, vital signs, hydration, urine output, fever, single-kidney history, pregnancy, and sepsis/obstruction signs.
Strain urine when ordered to capture the stone for analysis.
Escalate anuria, infected obstruction, uncontrolled pain/vomiting, or acute kidney injury.
assessMonitor: Trend pain, urine output, creatinine, fever, hydration, and ability to tolerate oral intake.
interventions: Provide prescribed analgesia, antiemetics, and fluids based on hydration status rather than forcing excessive fluid during acute obstruction.
Prepare for decompression or stone removal when obstruction or stone characteristics require intervention.
medicationSafety: NSAIDs are effective for renal colic in many patients but may be inappropriate with significant kidney dysfunction, GI bleeding risk, or other contraindications.
Alpha blockers may be prescribed for selected ureteral stones and can cause dizziness or hypotension.
teaching: Hydration for prevention is usually helpful when not contraindicated, but prevention should be tailored to stone type and medical history.
delegationScope: Urine straining and output measurement may be delegated with instructions; fever, anuria, or worsening pain requires licensed-nurse reassessment.
examTrap: Encouraging the patient to rapidly drink liters of water despite severe obstruction and persistent vomiting.
oneLinePearl: Stone pain is common; stone plus infection or anuria is the emergency.
sourceBasis: American Urological Association Kidney Stone Guidance

title: Urinary Retention and BPH: Drain Safely, Find the Cause
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Acute urinary retention presents with inability to void, suprapubic pain/distention, or overflow dribbling and can injure the kidneys. Confirm bladder distention, identify medication/neurologic/obstructive causes, and decompress with catheterization when ordered while monitoring for hematuria, hypotension, and post-obstructive diuresis in high-volume retention.
recognize: BPH commonly causes hesitancy, weak stream, incomplete emptying, nocturia, and retention in older men.
Anticholinergics, antihistamines, opioids, anesthesia, constipation, neurologic disease, and urethral obstruction can contribute.
Overflow incontinence may actually represent chronic retention.
priorities: Assess last void, bladder distention, pain, output, medications, constipation, neurologic symptoms, and infection signs.
Use bladder scan when available and ordered.
Escalate retention with acute kidney injury, fever/sepsis, gross hematuria/clots, or neurologic deficits.
assessMonitor: Measure catheter output, urine characteristics, BP, hydration, and renal function when retention was severe or prolonged.
interventions: Insert and secure urinary catheter using sterile technique when ordered and within scope.
Maintain unobstructed drainage and remove the catheter as soon as clinically appropriate.
medicationSafety: Alpha-1 blockers can cause orthostatic hypotension.
5-alpha-reductase inhibitors work slowly and are not rescue treatment for acute retention.
Decongestants and anticholinergic drugs can worsen retention in susceptible patients.
redFlags: New saddle anesthesia or leg weakness
teaching: Report inability to void, fever, worsening hematuria, or severe dizziness after starting alpha-blocker therapy.
delegationScope: Catheter insertion and bladder-scan authority varies by setting and state; follow policy.
Neurologic deficits or suspected obstructive AKI require immediate escalation.
examTrap: Treating overflow dribbling as simple incontinence without checking for a distended bladder.
oneLinePearl: A leaking bladder can still be a full bladder—think retention before incontinence.

title: Glomerulonephritis: Blood, Protein, Pressure, and Edema
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
bottomLine: Glomerular inflammation commonly produces hematuria, proteinuria, edema, hypertension, and reduced kidney function. The immediate nursing threats are fluid overload, severe hypertension, hyperkalemia, and rapidly declining renal function, not the urine color itself.
recognize: Tea- or cola-colored urine, periorbital edema, hypertension, and reduced urine output are classic nephritic clues.
Recent infection, autoimmune disease, vasculitis, or other systemic illness may be relevant.
Rapidly progressive disease can worsen kidney function over days to weeks.
priorities: Assess blood pressure, edema, lung sounds, weight, urine output, hematuria, and renal function.
Report pulmonary edema, severe hypertension, hyperkalemia, or rapid oliguria promptly.
Collect ordered urine and blood tests accurately.
assessMonitor: Trend creatinine/eGFR, potassium, urine protein/blood, blood pressure, daily weight, and fluid balance.
interventions: Implement prescribed sodium/fluid restrictions and antihypertensive or immunologic therapy based on cause.
Protect kidney function by avoiding nephrotoxins when possible.
medicationSafety: Immunosuppressive therapy, when used, raises infection risk and requires regimen-specific monitoring.
Diuretics can reduce edema but may worsen volume depletion if the patient is intravascularly depleted.
teaching: Keep follow-up urine and kidney-function testing and report declining urine output, worsening edema, dyspnea, or severe headache.
delegationScope: Weights and urine measurement may be delegated with explicit thresholds; worsening renal, respiratory, or neurologic findings require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Encouraging unlimited fluids because the urine looks concentrated despite edema and oliguria.
oneLinePearl: Nephritic pattern: blood, pressure, edema, and declining filtration.
sourceBasis: National Kidney Foundation Glomerular Disease Resources
